title: Physiology and mechanisms of labour
blurb: Explain how contractions build, define each stage of labour, and follow the baby's journey through the pelvis.
question: Mia, in her first labour at a birth centre, asks why her midwife keeps feeling her tummy and checking 'how low' the baby is. She also asks why the baby has to 'turn' to be born. How should the midwife explain the stages and mechanism of labour?

teach.h: Labour: a process the body drives
teach.body: Formally: labour is the process by which regular uterine contractions cause cervical change (position, consistency, effacement and dilatation) and the baby, placenta and membranes are expelled. NICE NG235 divides it into a latent and established first stage, a second stage and a third stage. In plain English: contractions open the cervix, then help push the baby down and out, then deliver the placenta. Each stage has its own normal pattern.

teach.caption: The loop amplifies itself until the baby and placenta are born and the stretch stops.

items.label: Contractions + cervical change up to 4 cm
Regular contractions, progressive dilatation from 4 cm
Baby visible, or pushing at full dilatation
Birth of baby to placenta and membranes

teach.h: Fetal skull: the diameter that presents
head: Attitude of head
Diameter
Length
teach.caption: Flexion presents the smallest diameter, which is why a well-flexed head progresses best.

teach.body: The pelvic inlet is widest from side to side (about 13 cm), but the outlet is widest from front to back (about 13 cm once the coccyx moves back, against about 11 cm between the ischial tuberosities). The head enters the brim with its long axis sideways, then internal rotation turns the occiput towards the symphysis pubis so the head's long diameter lines up with the outlet's widest diameter. After the head is born it restitutes, and external rotation brings the shoulders into the outlet's front-to-back diameter.

The midwife explains that abdominal palpation tells her the baby's lie, presentation, position and how many fifths of the head are still above the brim; a vaginal examination, with consent, adds dilatation, effacement, station (level of the head against the ischial spines), position, caput and moulding. Mia is 6 cm with regular contractions, so she is in established labour. The baby is tucking its chin and will turn to face her back to fit the pelvis.

teach.text: Two diameters of the same length: the BIPARIETAL diameter (about 9.5 cm) is the widest side-to-side diameter that engages; the SUBOCCIPITOBREGMATIC diameter (about 9.5 cm) is the front-to-back diameter that presents when the head is well flexed. And the latent stage runs up to 4 cm, not 3 cm.

items: Ferguson reflex: cervical stretch increases oxytocin release, strengthening contractions.
Latent: up to 4 cm; established: regular contractions and progressive dilatation from 4 cm.
First labour average 8 h (unlikely over 18); later labours average 5 h (unlikely over 12).
Second stage: passive (full, no pushing) and active (baby visible or pushing).
Flexed head presents suboccipitobregmatic 9.5 cm; brow presents mentovertical 13.5 cm.
Movements: engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution, external rotation.

summary: You can now explain how oxytocin and the Ferguson reflex drive labour, define each stage and its expected duration, and describe the cardinal movements. You can also link the fetal skull diameters and pelvic shape to why the baby flexes and rotates.

A.q: Which fetal skull diameter presents when the baby's head is well flexed in a vertex presentation?
A.why: Full flexion presents the smallest anteroposterior diameter, the suboccipitobregmatic (about 9.5 cm).

whyNot.0: The occipitofrontal diameter presents with a further deflexed head.
whyNot.2: The mentovertical diameter presents with an extended (brow) head.
whyNot.3: The suboccipitofrontal diameter presents when the head is deflexed.

A.q: After engagement and descent, in what order do the next three cardinal movements occur?
A.why: The sequence is engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution and external rotation.

whyNot.1: Extension is how the head is born, after flexion and rotation.

A.q: Which statement describes the Ferguson reflex in labour?
options: Oxytocin release falls as the cervix dilates
A.why: Pressure and stretch on the cervix send signals to the hypothalamus, causing more oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary and stronger contractions: a positive feedback loop.

whyNot.1: Oxytocin release rises, not falls, as stretch increases.
whyNot.2: Prolactin drives milk production, not contractions.
whyNot.3: Head pressure stimulates, rather than suppresses, oxytocin release.

B.q: How does NICE NG235 define the established first stage of labour?
options: Irregular contractions with dilatation up to 4 cm
Regular contractions and cervical dilatation from 3 cm onwards
Any contractions with full effacement of the cervix
Regular contractions with progressive dilatation from 4 cm
B.why: NG235 1.8.1: established first stage is regular contractions and progressive cervical dilatation from 4 cm.

whyNot.0: Contractions with change up to 4 cm describe the latent first stage.
whyNot.2: Effacement alone, without progressive dilatation, does not define established labour.

B.q: How does NICE NG235 define the third stage of labour?
options: From birth of the baby to expulsion of placenta and membranes
From full dilatation of the cervix to the birth of the baby
From the birth of the baby to the end of the first hour after
From clamping of the cord until the placenta separates
B.why: NG235 1.10.2: the third stage is the time from the birth of the baby to the expulsion of the placenta and membranes.

whyNot.2: The first hour after birth is not a stage of labour.
whyNot.3: The third stage begins at the birth, not at cord clamping, and ends with expulsion.

B.q: Freya, in her first labour, asks how long established labour usually lasts. What should the midwife tell her?
B.why: NG235 1.8.36: first labours last on average 8 hours and are unlikely to last over 18 hours.

whyNot.0: These figures apply to second and subsequent labours.
whyNot.1: These are not the NG235 figures.
whyNot.3: This greatly underestimates the length of a first labour.

C.q: Why does the fetal head rotate internally as it descends through the pelvis?
options: The inlet is widest from front to back
The outlet is widest from front to back
The outlet is widest from side to side
The ischial spines push the face forwards
C.why: The inlet is widest transversely (about 13 cm) but the outlet is widest anteroposteriorly (about 13 cm as the coccyx moves back, against about 11 cm transversely), so the head rotates to align its long diameter with the outlet.

whyNot.0: The inlet is widest transversely, not anteroposteriorly.
whyNot.3: Rotation brings the occiput, not the face, towards the symphysis.

C.q: Ellie, in her first labour at a freestanding midwifery unit, is contracting regularly. On palpation the baby's head is 5/5 palpable and free. What should the midwife do?
options: Perform an amniotomy to aid descent
C.why: NG235 1.8.11: a high (4/5 to 5/5 palpable) or free-floating head in a nulliparous woman is an indication for transfer to obstetric-led care.

whyNot.0: A free-floating head in a first labour is a listed transfer indication.
whyNot.1: Amniotomy with a high, mobile head risks cord prolapse.
whyNot.2: Waiting 4 hours delays transfer that NG235 recommends.

C.q: The baby's head is extended into a brow presentation. Which diameter presents to the pelvis?
C.why: An extended (brow) head presents the mentovertical diameter, about 13.5 cm, the largest of the skull diameters.

whyNot.1: The occipitofrontal diameter goes with a further deflexed vertex.
whyNot.2: The suboccipitofrontal diameter goes with a deflexed head.
whyNot.3: The suboccipitobregmatic diameter presents with a well-flexed head.

reteach.title: A key turning in a lock
reteach.question: Imagine the baby's head as an oval key and the pelvis as a lock whose slot changes direction. How does the key get through?

blocks.body: Tuck: the baby flexes its chin to its chest so the smallest part of the 'key' (9.5 cm) leads. Turn: the slot is sideways at the top of the pelvis and front-to-back at the bottom, so the head rotates as it descends. Lift: under the pubic arch the head extends and is born, then untwists and the shoulders turn to follow.

blocks.text: Remember: flexion first, then internal rotation, then extension. Extension is how the head is born, not how it enters.

explain.body: Latent first stage: contractions with some cervical change, including effacement and dilatation up to 4 cm, not necessarily continuous. Established: regular contractions and progressive dilatation from 4 cm.

test.q: Up to what cervical dilatation does NICE NG235 define the latent first stage of labour?
test.why: NG235 1.8.1: the latent first stage includes cervical change up to 4 cm.

whyNot.1: From 4 cm with regular contractions is established labour.
whyNot.3: 2 cm is below the NG235 cut-off.

explain.body: Oxytocin is released from the posterior pituitary. Stretch of the cervix signals the hypothalamus to release more, so contractions grow stronger and more frequent: positive feedback that stops once the baby and placenta are born.

test.q: From where is oxytocin released to drive uterine contractions?
test.why: Oxytocin is released from the posterior pituitary in response to hypothalamic signals.

whyNot.0: The anterior pituitary releases hormones such as prolactin, not oxytocin.
whyNot.2: The placenta does not release the oxytocin of the Ferguson reflex.
whyNot.3: The adrenal glands release adrenaline and cortisol, not oxytocin.

explain.body: Engagement is when the greatest transverse diameter of the fetal head, the biparietal diameter (about 9.5 cm), has passed through the pelvic inlet (brim).

test.q: What does it mean when the fetal head is engaged?
options: The head is visible at the vulva between contractions
The occiput has rotated round to lie under the symphysis
The head is 5/5 palpable on abdominal examination
Its widest transverse diameter has passed the brim
test.why: Engagement is when the biparietal diameter, the greatest transverse diameter, is at or has passed the pelvic inlet.

whyNot.0: A head visible at the vulva marks the active second stage.
whyNot.1: Rotation to the symphysis is internal rotation, which comes later.
whyNot.2: 5/5 palpable means the whole head is above the brim: not engaged.

explain.body: Station describes the level of the presenting part relative to the ischial spines of the pelvis, found on vaginal examination along with dilatation, effacement, position, caput and moulding.

test.q: Against which landmark is the station of the presenting part described?
test.why: Station is the level of the presenting part relative to the ischial spines (NG207 Bishop score definition; NG235 1.8.10).

whyNot.1: Abdominal fifths describe the head relative to the brim; station uses the spines.
whyNot.2: The sacral promontory is used in pelvic measurement, not station.
whyNot.3: The symphysis is a landmark for rotation, not station.
